subject: english-language

moments.title: Language and Woman's Place
moments.body: 1975: Robin Lakoff's 'Language and Woman's Place' published. Lakoff argues women's language is characterised by hedges, tag questions, intensifiers, polite forms, hypercorrect grammar, and 'empty' adjectives ('lovely', 'divine'). The features reflect (and reinforce) women's subordinate social position.
moments.takeaway: Lakoff's account was based partly on introspection and observation rather than systematic data. It opened the field even as later research refined or rejected its specific claims.

moments.title: Tannen's You Just Don't Understand
moments.body: 1990: Tannen's 'You Just Don't Understand: Women and Men in Conversation' becomes a bestseller. The 'difference' approach: women and men use language in different ways (Tannen frames them as different 'cultures'). Critics (Deborah Cameron) argue the framework downplays power asymmetries.
moments.takeaway: Tannen's accessible writing took gender linguistics to mass audiences. Whether it overstates difference is debated.

moments.title: Critique and refinement
moments.who: Janet Holmes, Penelope Eckert, Deborah Cameron, Mary Bucholtz
moments.body: 1992: Holmes's research challenges Lakoff's claims about tag questions (which serve multiple functions). Cameron's 'The Myth of Mars and Venus' (2007) critiques the difference approach. Eckert and McConnell-Ginet's 'Language and Gender' (2003) presents a more nuanced framework.
moments.takeaway: Modern gender linguistics is more contextual — gender is performed, varies by community, intersects with class, race, sexuality.

now.title: Gender in language now
now.body: Gendered linguistic patterns are real but more complex than the early models claimed. Trans linguistic studies, non-binary speakers, the relationship between gender expression and language all expand the field. Online gendered communication has generated its own subfield.
now.open_questions: Do women and men really speak differently? Yes on average and in specific patterns; no in ways that justify deterministic generalisation. Context, identity, situation all matter.

reflection: A 1975 book opened a field that has been continuously refined for nearly 50 years. Lakoff's claims have been substantially modified, but the question — how does gender structure language use? — has continued to organise productive research and contested public conversation.
